title: GPT-4 as a Homework Tutor can Improve Student Engagement and Learning Outcomes
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether GPT-4 can serve as an effective homework tutor in a real secondary-school setting, addressing the problem that homework often lacks timely feedback and follow-up support. The authors position LLM-based tutoring as a potentially scalable alternative to private tutoring or more labor-intensive intelligent tutoring systems, especially for language learning. They specifically investigate whether replacing traditional English homework with interactive GPT-4 tutoring can improve student engagement and learning outcomes.

The intervention used a prompting strategy that required teachers to provide only three elements for each homework assignment: its purpose, a task description, and an example. GPT-4 was then prompted to generate an interactive tutoring session aligned with the teacher’s pedagogical goals. Students in the treatment condition completed homework through a dedicated website where they interacted with GPT-4, while control students completed standard homework tasks. The study used pre/post tests, weekly surveys, and initial/final questionnaires to assess learning gains, engagement, satisfaction, and perceptions of support.

The study was conducted in one technical high school in Italy with four English classes taught by the same teacher: two 3rd-year classes and two 5th-year classes, with a total of 75 students. Students were randomly assigned within class to treatment or control using stratified randomization based on self-reported English GPA. The intervention targeted English as a second language homework, with students accessing the system outside school hours on their own devices. The planned 6-week intervention was extended to 8 weeks.

The authors conclude that GPT-4 homework tutoring improved student engagement and yielded some learning benefits, especially for 3rd-year students doing more objective grammar-focused homework. Students in the treatment group reported homework as more interesting and felt they had more resources available, and most wanted to continue using the tutor after the study. The paper also reports a low observed error rate in tutor interactions and finds no evidence that only stronger students benefited. However, effects on learning were limited overall, especially for 5th-year students, and the study emphasizes the promise of GPT-4 as a practical, minimally disruptive support tool rather than a full replacement for human instruction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family conversational large language model used here as an interactive homework tutor.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper used GPT-4 (gpt-4-0125-preview), delivered through a custom website, to replace traditional English homework with interactive tutoring sessions for Italian high-school students learning English as a second language.

findings.finding_summary: In the randomized controlled trial, overall learning gains favored the treatment group but were not statistically significant when pooling cohorts (Cohen's d=0.251, p=0.314). When analyzed by cohort, the 3rd year classes showed a larger, marginally significant advantage for GPT-4 homework tutoring (d=0.603, p=0.087), while the 5th year classes showed essentially no difference (d=-0.004, p=0.991).
findings.measure: Pre-test/post-test learning gains on 24-item multiple-choice English assessments
findings.effect_size: d=0.251 overall; d=0.603 (3rd year); d=-0.004 (5th year)

findings.finding_summary: Students in the treatment group rated homework as significantly more interesting than controls, with a medium effect size (d=0.593, p=0.011). The authors interpret this as improved short-term engagement with homework when GPT-4 replaced static assignments.
findings.measure: Weekly questionnaire rating of homework interestingness

findings.finding_summary: Students in the treatment condition reported significantly higher perceived availability of resources for completing exercises than controls (d=0.586, p=0.015). This suggests GPT-4 made students feel better supported during homework completion.

Students rated GPT-4 homework as more useful than traditional homework, but the difference was not statistically significant (d=0.356, p=0.125). The direction favored the treatment group, indicating a positive but inconclusive perceived utility effect.

Students rated GPT-4-supported exercises as more comprehensive than control homework, but the difference was not statistically significant (d=0.281, p=0.234). This indicates a positive but statistically inconclusive trend in perceived comprehensiveness.

Final survey responses showed high student acceptance and satisfaction with the tutor. Specifically, 32/33 respondents said the tutor helped them with homework, 30/35 said it improved them on a practical level, 26/34 said it helped them keep up with the English program, and 32/35 wanted to continue using it.
findings.measure: Final questionnaire perceptions of helpfulness, practical improvement, ability to keep up, and willingness to continue use

quality_tier_rationale: This is a real-world randomized controlled trial in four high-school classes with treatment and control conditions, which is stronger than correlational evidence. However, the sample is modest, several outcomes are self-reported, and the primary academic effect is only marginally significant in one cohort and null in another.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports medium-sized positive effects on engagement-related outcomes (d=0.593 and d=0.586) and a medium academic effect in the 3rd year subgroup (d=0.603), even though overall academic effects are mixed. Because reported effect sizes reach or exceed 0.20, the impact tier is blue.
